title.en: Diarmuid's Trick Feats Kill the Green Champions
title.zh: 迪爾穆德的技戲誅殺綠衣勇士

region.en: Marsh of Finnliath, Co. Mayo, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭梅奧郡芬利阿沼澤（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: Sent by Finn to hunt the fugitive, the Green Champions of Muir-na-locht — two thousand men with three hounds fire cannot burn nor water drown — meet a fighting man who claims to have seen Diarmuid yesterday. Diarmuid rolls a tun of wine down the hill with men crushed beneath it, lights on the point of Manannan's upturned spear like a bird, and walks thrice along the edge of Angus's sword; each feat is copied to death, fifty in the wine alone.
summary.zh: 芬恩遣「穆爾納赫特綠衣勇士」——兩千戰士與三隻火不能焚、水不能溺的魔犬——追捕逃亡者；他們遇上一名自稱昨日見過迪爾穆德的戰士。迪爾穆德滾酒桶下山、壓斃模仿者，如飛鳥般立於瑪那南倒插長矛之尖，並在安古斯之劍刃上三度行走——每一次技戲皆被依樣模仿而死，僅酒桶一項已斃五十人。

sensitivity.note: The lethal-feat mimicry (hostiles die copying the hero's tricks) is a fixed chase-tale device of the Diarmuid pursuit; the weapons named — Crann Buidhe of Manannan, Mor-alltach of Angus, Gae Buidhe/Gae Dearg — are Diarmuid's charter arms from his god-fosterers. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Diarmuid went up on a hill that was near, and saw a great fleet of ships coming from the west, and when they were come to land, nine times nine of the chief men came on shore. "Three kings we are of the Green Champions of Muir-na-locht, and Finn, son of Cumhal, sent looking for us by cause of a thief of the woods, and an enemy of his own that has gone hiding from him. We are twenty hundred good fighting men, and every one of us is a match for a hundred, and we have three deadly hounds with us; fire will not burn them, and water will not drown them, and arms will not redden on them." "I saw him yesterday," said Diarmuid, "and I myself am but a fighting man. And by my word, you will know Diarmuid's hand when you will meet it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Is there wine in your ships? If you have a mind to bring out a tun of wine, I will do a trick for you." Diarmuid took the tun between his two hands and drank a drink out of it, and brought it to the top of the hill, and went up himself on the tun, and let it go down the steep of the hill till it was at the bottom; and he did that trick three times before the strangers. But they said he was a man had never seen a good trick when he called that a trick; and with that a man of them went up on the tun, but Diarmuid gave a stroke of his foot at it and the young man fell from it before it began to move, and it rolled over him and crushed him, that he died. Another man went on it, and another after him again, till fifty of them were killed trying to do Diarmuid's trick. And the next day he put off his arms, all but the shirt next his skin, and struck the Crann Buidhe, the spear of Manannan, into the earth with the point upwards, and rose with a leap and lit on the point of the spear as light as a bird, and came down off it again without a wound on him — and a young man of the Green Champions came down heavily on the point, and it went through his heart. And the third day he put the sword of Angus Og, the Mor-alltach, between two forked poles on its edge, and walked on the sword three times from the hilt to the point, and came down and asked was there a man of them could do that feat; and a man rose up to walk on the sword, but came down heavily on it the way he was cut in two halves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: Three Kings Die in Diarmuid's Bonds
title.zh: 三王死於迪爾穆德之縛

region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡盧赫拉山

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: After the Green Champions fall, Diarmuid binds their three kings and leaves them alive, knowing only four men — Oisin, Osgar, Lugaidh's Son and Conan — can loosen bonds he tied. Muadhan's belt-whelp leaps into the first hound's throat; the Red Spear brings out the second's bowels; the third Diarmuid dashes its brains on the flagstone of Dubhan, then casts down the troop with the Gae Dearg. Finn's woman-messenger of the Black Mountain reports it all, and the three kings die under the hardness of the bonds.
summary.zh: 綠衣勇士潰滅後，迪爾穆德生擒並縛其三王——他知道僅有奧辛、奧斯加、盧蓋德之子、科南四人能解他所縛之縛。穆阿丹腰帶中的幼犬躍入第一隻魔犬咽喉；紅矛穿出第二隻內臟；第三隻被他在杜班石上撞破頭顱，繼而紅矛連誅三將。芬恩的「黑山信使」回報一切，三王竟死於堅不可解的束縛之中。

sensitivity.note: The unloosenable bonds (only four named looser-men) are a legalistic chain-of-bonds device characteristic of the cycle's geis logic; Muadhan's belt-whelp parallels Bran's whelp-rearing. The messenger-woman (fast as a weasel) repeats the cycle's shape-shifting courier pattern.

passages.text: Diarmuid drew his sword the Mor-alltach out of its sheath, and he made a fierce blow at the head nearest him that put it in two halves. Then he made an attack on the whole host of the Green Champions, and began to destroy them, cutting through the beautiful shining armour of the men of Muir-na-locht till there was hardly a man that could go back to give news of the fight, but only the three kings and a few of their people. He put his battle clothes on him, that no weapon could go through, and took the sword of Angus, that left no leavings after it, at his left side, and his two thick-handled spears, the Gae Buidhe and the Gae Dearg, the Yellow and the Red, that gave wounds there was no healing for; and he bound the three kings fast and firm: "There is no man of the heroes of Ireland can loosen those bonds but four only, Oisin, son of Finn, and Osgar, son of Oisin, and Lugaidh's Son of the Strong Hand, and Conan, son of Morna; and I know well none of those four will do it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: They brought their three hounds out of the ship and laid them on Diarmuid's track, and when he saw them coming like that he was filled with great hatred of them. Then Muadhan turned back, and took a whelp out of his belt, and put it on the flat of his hand; and when the whelp saw the hound rushing towards him, and its jaws open, he rose up and made a leap from Muadhan's hand into the throat of the hound, and came out of its side, bringing the heart with it, and left the hound dead after him. Another hound was loosened after them, and Diarmuid said: "I often heard there is nothing can stand against weapons of Druid wounding," and he made a cast at the hound, and the spear went through its body and brought out its bowels. The third hound overtook them at Lic Dhubhain, the flag-stone of Dubhan, on Slieve Luachra; Diarmuid took him by the two hind legs, and struck a blow of his carcase against the side of the rock till he had let out his brains through the openings of his head and of his ears. Then he made a good cast at the young man of the green cloak that was at the head of the troop, and killed him, and the second man, and the third man in the same way. And when Finn heard of the Kings of the Green Champions that were bound by Diarmuid, neither Oisin nor Osgar nor Conan nor Lugaidh's Son would loosen them; and they were not long talking about it till the three kings died under the hardness of the bonds that were on them. Then Finn made three wide-sodded graves for them, and a flag-stone was put over them, and another stone raised over that again, and their names were written in branching Ogham.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Rowan of Dubhros and the Hurling-Match of the Gods
title.zh: 杜布羅斯的花楸與神族擲球賽

region.en: Wood of Dubhros, Ui Fiachrach, Co. Mayo, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭梅奧郡杜布羅斯林地

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Two daughters of Manannan quarrel over whose man is the better hurler, and the match between the Men of Dea and the Fianna runs three days and nights without a goal. Passing homeward through Ui Fiachrach, the gods drop a rowan berry of the Land of the Ever-Living Living Ones, and a tree springs up whose berries banish sickness, make the hundred-year-old young again, and turn any girl into a flower of beauty — a tree the Tuatha de Danaan must guard with the Surly One of Lochlann, a giant with one eye and a prophecy that he will not die till three strokes of his own iron club fall on himself.
summary.zh: 瑪那南的兩位女兒為誰的情人更善擲球而爭執，神族與菲亞納之賽遂歷時三日三夜不分勝負。神族歸途經過伊·菲赫拉赫時失落一顆「永生者之國」的花楸果，樹從果中生——食其果者百病不侵，百歲老人可返少年，少女可成絕色。神族不得不以獨眼巨人格瓦恩看守此樹——預言曰：唯有親受自己鐵棒三擊者方能殺他。

sensitivity.note: The rejuvenating rowan is the Fenian apple-of-immortality (Berries of the Land of Promise) — compare Goibniu's ale and Idunn's apples cross-traditionally; the hurling-match of gods and men is a distinctive Irish divine-game motif. Coordinates at the traditional Dubhros (Doo Lough) country.

passages.text: There rose a dispute one time between two women of the Tuatha de Danaan, Aine and Aoife, daughters of Manannan, son of Lir, for Aoife had given her love to Lugaidh's Son, and Aine had given her love to a man of her own race, and each of them said her own man was a better hurler than the other. It came from that dispute that there was a great hurling match settled between the Men of Dea and the Fianna of Ireland, on a beautiful plain near Loch Lein. The highest men and the most daring of the Tuatha de Danaan were there — the three Garbhs of Slieve Mis, and the three Mases of Slieve Luachra, and the three yellow-haired Murchadhs, and Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, and Manannan, son of Lir; and they themselves and the Fianna were playing the match through the length of three days and three nights, and neither of them winning a goal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now the provision the Men of Dea had brought with them from the Land of Promise was crimson nuts, and apples, and sweet-smelling rowan berries. And as they were passing through the district of Ui Fiachrach by the Muaidh, a berry of the rowan berries fell from them, and a tree grew up from it. And there was virtue in its berries, and no sickness or disease would ever come on any person that would eat them, and those that would eat them would feel the liveliness of wine and the satisfaction of mead in them, and any old person of a hundred years that would eat them would go back to be young again, and any young girl that would eat them would grow to be a flower of beauty. And it is what they agreed, to send a young man of them in search of a man of Lochlann that would guard the tree by day and sleep in it by night; and his name was the Searbhan Lochlannach, the Surly One of Lochlann. Very black and ugly he was, having crooked teeth, and one eye only in the middle of his forehead. And he had a thick collar of iron around his body, and it was in the prophecy that he would never die till there would be three strokes of the iron club he had, struck upon himself.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: The Surly One of Lochlann Dies by His Own Club

region.en: Wood of Dubhros, Ui Fiachrach, Co. Mayo, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭梅奧郡杜布羅斯林地

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Finn sets two sons of Morna, children of his father's killers, the price of peace: Diarmuid's head or a fistful of the quicken berries of Dubhros. Oisin warns them of both; they choose to fight for Diarmuid's berries instead, and are bound by him. Grania will not live without the berries, so Diarmuid wakes the Surly One, takes his three blows on the shield, then seizes the iron club and strikes three great blows on the giant — putting his brains out through his head, fulfilling the prophecy.
summary.zh: 芬恩向弒父仇人莫爾納之子索和，開價：迪爾穆德之頭，或一把杜布羅斯花楸果。歐辛警告二者皆不可得；他們選擇為迪爾穆德求果，反遭其縛。格拉尼亞誓言無果不活，迪爾穆德遂喚醒悍翁，先受其三擊於盾上，繼而奪其鐵棒，反擊三棒——巨漿迸腦而出，預言應驗。

sensitivity.note: Self-inflicted fatal blows fulfilling a prophecy is the classic paradoxical-death motif (cf. Balor's eye under Lug, Rhiannon's birds); the 'fine of peace' demanded of orphans of old enemies is a legal-fiction of Irish feud-settlement. Same pin as the rowan record.

passages.text: Finn and his people were not long at Almhuin till they saw fifty armed men coming towards them: "We are enemies of your own, and our fathers were at the killing of your father, and they themselves died for that deed. And it is to ask peace we are come now to you." "I must put a fine on you first in satisfaction for my father's death. I am asking but the head of a champion, or the full of a fist of the berries of the quicken-tree at Dubhros." "I will give you a good advice, children of Morna, to go back to the place you were reared, and not to ask peace of Finn through the length of your lives. For do you know whose head he is asking you to bring him? The head of Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne; and if you were twenty hundred men in their full strength, Diarmuid would not let you take that head."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Although the children of Morna do not go looking for those berries, I will not lie in a bed for ever till I get a share of them," said Grania, "and I will not live if I do not get them." Then Diarmuid went to the Surly One, and gave him a stroke of his foot, and said: "It is Grania, daughter of the High King, has a desire to taste those berries, and it is to ask a handful of them I am come." "If she is to die for it, she will never taste a berry of those berries." "Willing or unwilling, I will take those berries from you." When the Surly One heard that, he rose up on his feet and lifted his club and struck three great blows on Diarmuid, that gave him some little hurt in spite of his shield. But when Diarmuid saw him not minding himself, he threw down his weapons, and made a great leap and took hold of the club with his two hands. And when he had a hold of the club he struck three great blows on him that put his brains out through his head. And when they saw the Surly One was killed, Diarmuid plucked the berries for Grania and for the children of Morna, and they ate their fill of them, and the two young men went back to where Finn was with the load Diarmuid plucked for them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. IV; not verbatim.
